prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, a new regime of precision measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: I keep B007 with Katori and Ye as a single-part prize. Having now read all eight round-1 statements, my judgement rests on three points that do not depend on counting support. First, the invention is specific and decisive: the magic-wavelength condition removes the light shift of the clock transition by design, which is what allows thousands of neutral atoms to be interrogated at once. Second, the result has been confirmed independently, which is the test I apply to any instrument. Several laboratories have built and intercompared lattice clocks at the 1e-18 level, and the clocks already return physics: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on variation of constants and dark-matter searches. Third, the credit is as clean as anything on the shortlist, with two names that all six B007 supporters share and no one has proposed to change. The strongest argument against is category, not science, and I answer it below. I regard the SI second as a question of timing, not of scientific merit: the committee can assess a measurement capability that has already been realised and reproduced, whether or not the metrology bodies have redefined the unit.
statement.case_against: The main objection stands. A clock can be read as an instrument advance that continues the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems. I do not find that objection decisive, since neither earlier prize covered trapping many neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice, but a fair colleague can weigh it differently, and I will not pretend it is settled. Credit is the second weakness: Lemonde's early strontium work, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the JILA team, and the ion-clock groups are outside two names, and several of us, myself included, rely on recollection of the priority history and not on checked documents. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so part of the impact is still prospective. B001 is the real competitor, and its weaknesses (unresolved pairing mechanism, device variation, the omission of Cao and earlier twisted-bilayer theory) are mostly about a young field, not about a lack of science.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B001 and concedes that the optical lattice clock is further along in maturity with cleaner attribution, while ranking it fifth because of possible overlap with earlier metrology prizes.
responses.response: Your own statement gives the maturity and attribution point to B007, and I think that matters. On overlap, I would ask you what in the 2005 or 2012 citation would cover the lattice clock. The comb prize recognised the frequency-measurement tool and the 2012 prize recognised quantum control of single ions. A neutral-atom clock with magic wavelengths is a different physical solution to the systematic-shift problem. I accept that B001 shows a better theory-experiment loop, and that is a legitimate reason to place it first, but your two reservations (pairing mechanism, twist-angle disorder) are ones I would weigh as real maturity costs. If an expert report cleared the credit for Cao and for earlier theory I would rank B001 close to B007, and I regard it as the right alternative, not as a weaker one.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether a prize before the redefinition of the second is timely or slightly early, and notes that B007 pairs poorly with any second part because only one name would remain.
responses.response: On timing, I think the redefinition is evidence of acceptance but not a condition for the physics: the performance is reproduced and intercompared today. If we waited for the unit to change we would be making a decision about metrology bodies, not about the science. On configuration I agree with you, and it is the reason I do not propose a second part. None of the other candidates fits one remaining name, and adding a part would only force us to cut Katori or Ye. Your disclosure about the year in John Hall's laboratory is worth the committee noting. I do not see it as a conflict for you, and it is a reason to want the priority history checked by an outside expert so that nobody's recollection decides it.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the discovery in B007 is the demonstrated ability to cancel systematic shifts for thousands of atoms at once, and that a citation can be written without overlap with 2005 and 2012, while conceding that colleagues may weigh it as precision metrology and that credit for Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley rests on recollection.
responses.response: I agree with the framing and have tried to put it in the citation by naming the invention and the new regime of precision, and not a single application. As Secretary you are best placed to request the expert report. My answer to the chair's own question about the historical record is that it needs to establish three things: who first proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and when, who first demonstrated the lattice clock at the precision that others then reproduced, and whether any ion-clock or SYRTE contribution was so entangled with those steps that a two-name award would misrepresent them. If it finds that, I would want the committee to say so openly and not to add names at the cost of exceeding three.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B001 for its analytically transparent continuum model and sharp prediction, but states that if the committee finds the discovery not yet settled, the optical lattice clock is the more mature and less contested choice.
responses.response: That conditional is the argument I would make to a sceptical colleague, and I am glad to see it from a B001 supporter. I take your point that a transparent model with a sharp prediction is a strong kind of discovery, and I cannot judge the condensed-matter physics myself. What I can say as an experimentalist is that the unresolved pairing mechanism, disorder between devices and the open credit question for the first experimental authors are all features that make the three-name configuration harder to defend this year. Because both of us name the other as the fallback, I read our difference as one of maturity and credit risk, not as a scientific dispute. I would reconsider only if the experts show that the B001 credit gap can be handled within three names.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B007, weighs the pending redefinition of the second and has flagged a University of Tokyo fellowship, with no apparent connection to Katori or Ye.
responses.response: Your disclosure is the right one to make and I agree with how you frame it, as an institutional association without a research link to the candidates. I also note that you and I reached B007 from different starting points, you from an instrument-invention view that also favoured B030 and I from the criterion of independent confirmation, which makes the agreement more informative than a shared first impression. Your question to the committee about maturity I answer as above. On B030, I still see a credit problem in the corrector pioneers and a lack of support elsewhere, so I do not see it reinstated this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a distinct achievement from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes, a judgement I cannot settle with facts.

Whether the priority history supports exactly Katori and Ye. I rely on recollection and would want an expert report on the first magic-wavelength proposal and the first reproduced high-precision lattice clocks.
Whether B001 should come first if experts confirm its credit history; I cannot assess the condensed-matter physics independently and defer to Eriksson and Mehlig on that.
IceCube (B039), my opening first choice, still needs a defensible three-name split in a large collaboration, with source associations not yet independently confirmed.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict on B007 or B001. For disclosure, I belong to the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, and IceCube (B039) is in my broad field of astroparticle physics, but I have no collaboration with IceCube or its credited individuals. I note that Kroll's year in John Hall's laboratory and Olsson's Tokyo fellowship are disclosed and do not alter my view of them as discussants.
